Ramée) comments: ‘In that most beautiful and too little known of poems, “Epipsychidion,” the whole
scene, though called Greek, is Italian, and might be taken from the woods beside the Lake of Garda, or
the Sercchio which he knew so well, or the forest-like parks which lie deep and cool and still in the blue
shadows of Appenine or Abruzzi’ (‘Shelley’, in Views and Opinions (1895) 254–80 (267–8)).
 for] because.
 pastoral] Either in the sense of ‘caring for flocks or herds’ or ‘rustic’ (as in l. 485); the gloss in
Concordance is ‘rustic, rural’.
 the age of gold] The mythical Golden Age as described in e.g. Hesiod, Works and Days 106ff. and
Ovid, Met. i 89ff. In Peacock’s essay The Four Ages of Poetry which S. appears to have read shortly before
20 January 1821 (see L ii 257–8), Peacock described the ‘golden age of poetry’ as one in which (‘Men . . .
 live[d] . . . more in the light of truth’ (Peacock Works viii 6–7).
